books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: Thomas Cole's The Oxbow (View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm), painted in 1836, looks down from a high, storm-darkened hillside. On the left, a gnarled tree leans over wild forest under black clouds. On the right, the Connecticut River bends through sunny, cleared farmland dotted with fields and small boats. A tiny figure with an easel stands on the rocks at lower right.
stimulus.source_note: Painting: Thomas Cole, The Oxbow, 1836 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain; image viewed before writing. Description records only what the painting visibly shows.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Cole's tiny figure with an easel at lower right most likely shows which of the following?

options.text: The painter was paid by the farmers whose land he painted
options.misconception: The figure stands near the farmland, so it is easy to assume the farmers hired him.

options.text: The scene was painted outdoors in a single stormy afternoon
options.misconception: The storm looks freshly observed, so it is easy to think Cole finished it on the spot.

options.text: Cole thought artists should stay out of nature entirely
options.misconception: The figure is so small that it is easy to read it as unimportant or unwelcome.

options.text: The artist placing himself inside the landscape, watching civilization meet wilderness

rationales.A: Nothing in the painting says who paid Cole; the figure is an artist at work, not a receipt.
rationales.B: A canvas this large was finished in the studio from sketches, not in one afternoon on a hilltop.
rationales.C: The figure is painting the view, not avoiding it; Cole put himself in the scene on purpose.
rationales.D: The tiny easel figure is Cole himself, standing where wild land and farmed land meet.
rationales.general:
1. Find the figure. The stimulus places a tiny artist with an easel on the rocks at lower right.
2. Ask why Cole shrank himself into his own painting. He is a witness, small against the land, watching the change.
Background: Hudson River School painters often set small figures in vast nature to show its scale.
Remember: a tiny figure in a huge landscape is usually there to show you how big the land is.

figures.caption: Thomas Cole, The Oxbow, 1836. Stormy wilderness at left, sunny farmland at right.
figures.alt: Thomas Cole's 1836 painting The Oxbow: a storm-darkened wooded hillside at left, the Connecticut River bending through sunny farmland at right, a tiny artist with an easel on the rocks below
